records.name_note: NC State Extension's plant record lists "Previously known as: Iberis commutata" — i.e. Iberis commutata is the older synonym and Iberis sempervirens (the name given) is the current accepted binomial. No other admissible source suggested a different accepted name, so no conflict.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: none of the admissible sources address toxicity to pets or humans for Iberis sempervirens — NC State Extension's normal Toxicity section is absent from this species' page, and RHS, Clemson HGIC, and Missouri Botanical Garden give no toxicity/poisonous language anywhere on their pages. Left null rather than inferring from the Brassicaceae family.

chill_damage_f: sources (NC State, Clemson, MOBOT) recommend winter mulch to prevent 'winter damage' and sun-scorch/desiccation in cold climates, but none state the actual temperature at which cold damage begins — only a general cold-protection practice.

day_f_min/day_f_max, night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source states specific day or night temperature ranges in °F. Sources give only USDA hardiness zone ranges (e.g. NC State: 3a–8b; Clemson: 3–9; MOBOT: 3–8), which is a survival-zone figure, not a day/night comfort range, and there's no field for it in this schema.

light_fc_min / light_fc_good: this is an outdoor garden perennial and all sources describe light by duration/category (full sun vs. part/light shade) rather than footcandle intensity, per the field notes for outdoor plants.
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source.

soil_ph_max: NC State's categorical soil-pH scheme lists the plant as tolerating 'Alkaline (>8.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' — the alkaline category is open-ended with no stated upper bound, so only the lower bound (6.0) could be sourced as a number.

water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis / water_check_depth_cm / water_dry_down_target: no admissible source gives day-interval or soil-depth-based watering guidance for this species.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_strength: Clemson HGIC gives specific calendar timing (early-to-mid March and September) and a per-area application rate (1 lb, then ½ lb per 100 sq ft), but not a day-count interval or a full/half/quarter dilution-strength category.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State and Clemson both define 'full sun' as a minimum threshold ('6 or more hours' / 'greater than 6 hours' of direct sunlight) for the exposure category — that's a floor, not a stated maximum tolerated, so it wasn't mapped to this field.

water_regime — removed on audit: Value 'dry_surface_between' overstates dryness beyond what the cited sources say for this species. Clemson's own quote is 'moist to slightly dry conditions' (average-leaning, not a let-the-surface-dry-out regime), and Missouri Botanical Garden's page carries its own STRUCTURED attribute 'Water: Medium' immediately adjacent to the prose the record quoted ('Typically grown in medium moisture... Tolerant of drought') -- MOBOT's own Dry/Dry-to-medium/Medium/Medium-to-wet/Wet scale rates this plant 'Medium,' not a drought/xeric tier. The record cited only the prose and never reconciled it against MOBOT's own structured water tag or Clemson's non-committal phrasing -- the subtler case flagged in structural check 1, where a cited source's own structured field contradicts the prose quote actually used. Given the genuine tension between 'moist'-leaning primary language and a 'dry' categorical value, this should have been left null.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Value 'moderate' is not supported by any of the four sources, all of which converge on well-drained soil being a firm requirement with a stated failure mode. NC State's own structured field reads 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage Moist' (a 'Good Drainage' tag, not 'moderate'), RHS says 'Moist but well-drained,' MOBOT states 'Well-drained soil is the key to growing this plant well' and warns 'Crown rot may occur if grown in moist, poorly drained soils,' and Clemson recommends amending poor soils 'to enhance drainage' because the plant does 'not tolerate excessive moisture.' No source uses 'moderate' language for drainage; the record softened a unanimous well-drained-required signal into a category that could read as 'average garden soil is fine,' with a real plant-harm consequence (crown/root rot) if followed.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: Clemson describes one springtime (late March/early April) application of granular 12-6-6 slow-release fertilizer at 1 lb/100 sq ft, with no stated repeat interval and no full/half/quarter dilution framing, so neither field is supported.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source discusses a dormancy or cool-rest care period for this species.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Citation 3 quotes NC State as 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage Moist Occasionally Dry,' but the source's raw HTML <dt>Soil Drainage:</dt> block contains only two <dd> attributes -- 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist.' The string 'Dry' appears zero times anywhere on the page (verified against the full page text, not a summarized render). 'Occasionally Dry' was fabricated and added to the quote; it is exactly the tag used to justify averaging three drainage descriptors into a 'moderate' value. With the real evidence being only 'Good Drainage' + 'Moist' from NC State and 'evenly moist, well-drained' from Clemson -- no real source anywhere mentions dry tolerance -- the record leans toward a wetter classification than 'moderate' actually supports, on top of the citation itself misrepresenting its source.

unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no cited source gives explicit day- or night-specific temperature ranges; only a tuber cold-injury threshold was found (used for chill_damage_f).
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no cited source states a humidity requirement for this outdoor garden species.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: sources give a sun-duration category (full sun to partial shade) rather than a footcandle or hours-of-direct-sun number; captured instead via outdoor_sun_exposure per the field notes.
soil_base: sources describe soil qualities (fertile, moist, well-drained) but none frames dahlia's growing medium as a named potting/soil-mix category.
soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: UF/IFAS notes qualitative tolerance of 'acidic' and 'loam' soils but no source gives numeric pH figures.
fertilize_strength: Clemson gives a fertilizer schedule and rate (monthly, or 2-3 lb of 5-10-10/10-10-10 per 100 sq ft) but does not state a dilution strength relative to label rate.
fertilize_active_months: Clemson mentions a July application as one option within a 'fertilize monthly' schedule, but no source lists a specific set of active months.

water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_check_depth_cm/water_dry_down_target/water_estimate_basis: sources give only qualitative watering guidance ('plenty of water', 'thirsty plants', avoid waterlogging), captured in water_regime; no source gives a specific interval or check depth to estimate from.

toxicity_detail: NC State tags dahlia as a problem for cats, dogs, and horses (used for toxic_to_pets), but the page's detailed symptom/mechanism writeup - phototoxic dermatitis from handling, mild GI signs from leaf ingestion - is filed under 'Poisonous to Humans', not a pet-specific writeup, so it was not used here to avoid blending human-toxicity detail into a pet-toxicity field.

toxic_to_pets — removed on audit: Sole citation is NC State's genus-level Dahlia page, which I fetched directly: it says 'cultivated dahlias are hybrids of mixed parentage' and notes the entry was 'Previously known as Dahlia x hortensis' -- i.e. it is a page about garden hybrid dahlias in general, not the species Dahlia pinnata. The '#problem for cats/dogs/horses' tags are genuine pet-tags (not confused with the separate 'Poisonous to Humans' prose, which the record correctly kept out of toxicity_detail), so the tag itself is real -- but nothing on the page ties that tag to Dahlia pinnata specifically, and this is the single most harm-capable field in the record. RHS's actual Dahlia pinnata species page and its growing guide are both silent on toxicity (confirmed by fetch), so there is no species-specific corroboration anywhere in the citation set.

chill_damage_f — removed on audit: The 25 F figure is correctly quoted ('injured at temperatures below 25 degrees F' matches the label's 25 exactly), but it comes from the same NC State genus/hybrid-complex page ('cultivated dahlias are hybrids of mixed parentage', previously Dahlia x hortensis). A precise numeric cold-injury threshold is being presented as settled fact for the species Dahlia pinnata when the source never names or discusses that species -- it is describing garden hybrid stock broadly.

water_regime — removed on audit: Fetched the RHS growing-guide page directly: it never mentions Dahlia pinnata anywhere and explicitly frames itself around dahlias that 'have been widely bred to produce thousands of cultivars.' The moisture quote used ('won't thrive in very dry conditions... may rot in waterlogged soil') is generic garden-cultivar advice, not evidence specific to the species this record claims to describe.

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: The claim label states 30 (days), but the cited Clemson quote never contains that number -- it says 'Fertilize monthly ... or apply 2 to 3 pounds ... in July,' offering monthly water-soluble feeding as one option alongside a single granular application in July as an alternative. Translating 'monthly' to the literal number 30 without flagging that the source actually poses two different schedules is an unverified numeric conversion, and Clemson's own page captions this as generic 'Dahlia species' guidance, not Dahlia pinnata.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Both quotes actually used ('Good Drainage' from NC State's tag, 'free-draining' from RHS) describe well-drained/good-drainage soil, not the 'moderate' drainage category the record assigned -- the category label doesn't match what either quote literally says. On top of that, both sources are the same genus/hybrid-level pages flagged for chill_damage_f and water_regime, not Dahlia-pinnata-specific.

cool_rest_note — removed on audit: The 35-45 F tuber storage detail is quoted accurately, but its only source is NC State's genus/hybrid-complex Dahlia page (self-described as covering hybrids of mixed parentage, previously Dahlia x hortensis), so this describes common garden-hybrid tuber-storage practice rather than something verified for the species Dahlia pinnata.

unknowns: chill_damage_f: sources give only survival hardiness (USDA zones 5-9 per NC State; RHS H5 = -15 to -10C) which is a mature-plant survival floor, not the actionable frost/cold damage-onset temperature this field requires, so left null.

water_regime: sources disagree on water need level. Missouri Botanical Garden rates it 'Water: Dry to medium' and says wet winter soil 'can be fatal,' matching NC State's drought-tolerant/intolerant-of-wet note, while RHS's cultivation guidance calls for soil that is 'moist but well-drained.' These do not clearly resolve to one water_regime category, so left null rather than pick a side.

direct_sun_hours_max / light_fc_min / light_fc_good: no source gives a species-specific sun-hours or footcandle number. NC State's '6 or more hours' text is a site-wide boilerplate definition of its generic 'Full sun' category label (reused across unrelated plant pages), not a value stated specifically for this species, so it was not used as a numeric claim; sun need is instead captured via outdoor_sun_exposure.
soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: RHS lists pH tolerance only as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' (i.e., broadly tolerant of all) with no numeric bounds given, so no range could be extracted.
fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: none of the approved sources give a fertilizing schedule specific to this species.
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no approved source addresses humidity for this outdoor garden perennial.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, cool_rest_note: no source gives day/night temperature setpoints or dormancy/cool-rest guidance for this species; only broad winter-hardiness zone/rating figures are given, which answer a different question.

water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis / water_check_depth_cm / water_dry_down_target: no source gives a specific watering-interval day count or soil-check depth for this species.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Every substantive piece of toxicity_detail (the hypersalivation/mouth irritation/vomiting/diarrhea symptom list, the 'sesquiterpene lactones and pyrethrins' toxic principle, and the flowers/leaves/roots/stems part list) is drawn from NC State's page, but I fetched the raw HTML and confirmed all of it sits under a block explicitly headed Poisonous to Humans: (containing Poison Severity, Poison Symptoms, Poison Toxic Principle, Causes Contact Dermatitis, Poison Part — all under that heading, id="poison"). There is no separate 'Poisonous to Pets/Dogs/Cats' structured section anywhere on the page. The only content that actually names an animal is a bare, unelaborated tag list ('Problem for Cats', 'Problem for Dogs') with zero symptom or mechanism detail attached, plus one general species-specific sentence ('Shasta daisies are mildly toxic to humans and pets if ingested'). I cross-checked NC State's own template on a related species (Chrysanthemum x morifolium), which uses the identical 'Poisonous to Humans:' heading/structure for its own (different) symptom text, confirming this is a deliberate, consistent human-only categorization on NC State's site, not incidental phrasing. The record took the human-labeled mechanism/symptom data and presented it as the detail behind toxic_to_pets=true, which the source never establishes for animals specifically. A pet owner reading toxicity_detail would believe hypersalivation/vomiting/diarrhea and the sesquiterpene-lactone/pyrethrin mechanism are documented outcomes in dogs or cats, when NC State only documents that mechanism for humans and only tags (without elaborating) that the plant is a problem for cats and dogs.

toxicity_detail intentionally omits the human-specific symptom list (nausea, vomiting, irregular pulse, convulsions, etc.) that NC State scopes to its 'Poisonous to Humans' section, to avoid presenting human symptom data as if it described pets.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The 'cardiac glycosides' toxic-principle and 'toxic parts: flowers, leaves, roots, stems' data are drawn exclusively from NC State's structured toxicity block, which I confirmed via raw HTML inspection is wrapped entirely under a group header literally labeled `Poisonous to Humans:` -- Poison Severity, Poison Symptoms, Poison Toxic Principle, and Poison Part are all nested inside that single human-scoped block. NC State provides no separate structured toxicity block for animals anywhere on the page; 'Problem for Cats', 'Problem for Dogs', and 'Problem for Horses' are flat, undetailed tags in an unrelated 'Problems:' list with zero associated severity/principle/part data. The record's own unknowns note shows it recognized this exact scoping issue and deliberately excluded NC State's human symptom list ('nausea, vomiting... convulsions... death') as human-specific -- but it did not apply that same discipline to the toxic-principle and toxic-parts data, which comes from the identical 'Poisonous to Humans:'-headed block. The record instead presents 'cardiac glycosides' and the flowers/leaves/roots/stems part list as general, plant-wide facts implicitly supporting the pet-toxicity claim, when the source itself files that detail only under the human-toxicity heading, sitting directly beside the undetailed pet-specific tags. This is the exact 'subtler case' the audit's structural check #3 warns about: mechanism/part detail copied from a human-toxicity section of a source that happens to sit near a separate, undetailed pet-specific tag. (Note: toxic_to_pets itself is NOT refuted -- it is independently and directly supported by NC State's species-specific 'Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses' tags and by RHS's explicit, species-specific 'TOXIC to pets' statement, both verified against clean, identity-confirmed page fetches.)

normalizations: 2026-08-21: landed with zero manual fixes. Both species flagged in advance -- Foxglove (cardiac glycosides, one of the best-documented genuinely dangerous garden plants) and Delphinium (toxic alkaloids) -- correctly resolved toxic_to_pets=true, each grounded in genuinely pet-inclusive language (RHS's explicit 'TOXIC to pets' for Foxglove; RHS's 'Humans/Pets: Harmful if eaten' for Delphinium) rather than borrowed from a human-only section. Foxglove's audit went a level deeper than seen before: even the toxic-principle/plant-parts detail that looked properly structured turned out, on raw HTML inspection, to be nested entirely under a 'Poisonous to Humans' group header on the source page -- correctly stripped from toxicity_detail despite reading as legitimate mechanism data at a glance.

Candytuft's audit caught two costed-consequence errors: water_regime was set to a drier category than Clemson's own 'moist to slightly dry' phrasing supports, with Missouri Botanical Garden's structured 'Water: Medium' tag sitting right next to the prose the record actually quoted and never reconciled against it. soil_drainage was softened to 'moderate' against a unanimous well-drained-required signal across all four sources, with Missouri Botanical Garden and Clemson both naming the specific failure mode (crown/root rot) that following the softer reading risks causing.
